chapter: First jobs and New Orleans players
title: Favorite altos and playing the melody
summary: Few altos could hold the melody; he names Son Johnson, Eddie Johnson and himself, and says audiences wanted lead and harmony mixed.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: Who were some of your favorite musicians you liked those days that you would hear? On sax, for instance, was there any particular favorite that you had on either alto or tenor?

Well, I'll tell you, there are a lot of fellows that liked me on the alto. Because one thing about the alto at that particular time, it wasn't too many fellows that could keep the melody. So they only had about three of us that could keep that melody. If the fellows knew, one was Son Johnson and Eddie Johnson and me. We'd known that fellows that could play plenty of melody. You know the leads on all numbers. We'd take years ago, well, the musicians, they always did look up to the trumpet player for the leader. And more often after the trumpet would play the lead, well, some of the sikes, well, they would improvise. They didn't know too much melody, but we had certain jobs that people wanted the melody. Then if you improvise in between, they want you to get on the melody on and off. Then you're playing more Dixieland, what they can understand. But if you just go all out with this improvising, well, they don't know what you didn't play. But sometimes you can ask people to ask you to play a diamond. Well, if this come on out improvising, well, they don't hear the melody of it. They don't know what they didn't play. But probably another musician, he would understand the harmony. But everybody would understand harmony. So on the other hand, for the benefit of the doubt, you'd have to play a little lead and a little harmony. So they can understand what you're doing. But everybody would understand harmony. But a musician would.
